summary: Tackles differences between sites' tables of Host names and network addresses and proposes how to resolve them. It is one of several related early notes on providing host names on-line, alongside RFCs 608, 623, 625 and 627.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC proposes one on-line host list that computers could read. Each entry would give a host's name and address, with optional details about supported features.

subtitle: A proposal for an on-line file mapping official host names to addresses and attributes.

tldr.problem: Sites kept different and often outdated lists mapping host names to host addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The author proposes an on-line ASCII file maintained by the NIC, with a host name and address plus optional attribute-value pairs.
tldr.outcome: The file would provide a simple shared source of host information, not replace option negotiation or other ways hosts learn about each other.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 606 as Unknown, with no RFC recorded as updating or obsoleting it. The RFC proposes a shared host file and does not say whether it was adopted.

sections.title: One Shared Host List
sections.content:
L. Peter Deutsch says TENEX sites had different mappings between host names and addresses, and none was complete. Since the NIC maintained the official host list, he proposes that it also keep an on-line file accessible to network programs.

He argues that a machine-readable ASCII file would be more useful for programs than an NLS structured file that could not be accessed through the Network.
sections.plainLanguage: Different computers had different copies of the host list. The author asks the NIC to keep one shared copy that programs can read.

sections.title: Host Entries and Attributes
sections.content:
Each entry would contain the official host name and host address. Optional attributes could describe protocol choices, host functions, accepted nicknames, preferred FTP byte sizes, or whether a host expected local or remote echo.

The author says attributes would be optional and could be incomplete, because the file supplements rather than replaces negotiation and other information sources.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry starts with a name and address. Extra fields can describe useful details, but a host does not need to provide every field.

sections.title: The Proposed File Format
sections.content:
The suggested format is an ASCII property list. A basic line gives a host name and decimal address, followed by optional lines of the form attribute name equals attribute value; a blank line ends an entry.

The RFC points to RFC 597 for host-name form and suggests carriage return followed by line feed as the end-of-line convention.
sections.plainLanguage: The format uses readable lines that pair an attribute with its value. Programs could scan the file without relying on a value's position in a fixed table.
